sentences.text: Elaphrocnemus was an extinct bird that lived in Europe during the Eocene and Oligocene periods. Unlike its living relatives, this ancient creature was a significantly better flyer.

Its anatomy supported this ability, featuring long scapulas similar to those of pelicans and proportionally large, strong wing bones. Despite having a weakly developed furcula like modern seriemas, these adaptations made it an efficient aerialist.
This bird was one of the most common species in the Quercy Formation, possibly living in large flocks.
Unlike many of its kin, Elaphrocnemus had shorter legs, implying it was less adapted for running.
The genus Elaphrocnemus was first described by Milne-Edwards in 1891.
It lived in a subtropical climate that supported a rich rainforest ecosystem with diverse mammals and birds.
Elaphrocnemus belongs to the order Cariamiformes and is most closely related to modern seriemas.
It was originally placed in the family Orthocnemidae, which was later absorbed into Idiornithidae.
The classification of Elaphrocnemus is debated because recent studies suggest the family Idiornithidae is polyphyletic.
Some researchers consider Elaphrocnemus a synonym of Talantatos, while others treat it as a distinct genus.
Fossils of Elaphrocnemus date from the Middle Eocene to the Late Oligocene.
